citation: crates/muster-core/src/typeable.rs, crates/muster-seam/src/bridge_link.rs, and kan card a_27Y4QtzyK. There is no oracle above these: how long a pane may render before Muster accuses its bridge is Muster's call, and these cases are where it is written down. The five seconds the seam actually uses is argued from the contract tier, crates/muster-contract/tests/launch.rs, which gives a healthy launch 2.0s after `app.ready` for every bridge to start, attach and paint.
why:
A pane becomes typeable when its bridge says, on the socket Muster bound for it, that it has attached to the pane, and until then the pane shows what it last drew and nothing typed into it appears. Three separate bugs in this repo all ended in exactly that state - the bridge failed to dial, the socket path had moved, the channel could not be opened - and none of them said anything until somebody typed. Both ends of the wait are already known to the core, so the only thing missing was a deadline between them, which is what these cases pin.

Every case answers with the diff rather than the current set, because raising and clearing are the two things the caller can do, and getting the second one wrong is how a stale error outlives the pane it was about. Each clear also says why - `dialed`, `closed`, `hidden` or `restarted` - because the run log carries it, and a clear that cannot tell a bridge arriving from a pane nobody is drawing any more leaves a reader guessing which happened. `next_wake` is answered by every case too, because a loop around this has exactly two ways to go wrong: spinning on a pane it has already reported, and sleeping through one that fell overdue while it was busy elsewhere.

Times are nanoseconds, matching the monotonic clock the seam counts in. `raised` and `cleared` accumulate over every `reconcile` a case performs, so a case with two readings shows whether the second one had anything new to say. `next_wake` is asked once, at the case's `now` or at its last reading.

A wait starts either way a pane can be waiting: `opened` is a socket bound with no bridge yet, and `ended` is the same wait restarting after one stopped, carrying how it stopped. The second is why the sentence differs at all - a pane looks identical in every one of these cases and the thing to do differs in all of them, and until they were told apart every one of them read as `look in the run log`.

`showing` is the third thing a wait turns on, and it is the window rather than the clock: the panes it names are the ones a region is drawing, straight from `View::showing`. What this raises is that a pane shows nothing of what is typed into it, so a pane nothing is drawing has no such claim to make - and a pane drawn again waits a whole deadline from the moment it is drawn, because its clock ran while nobody could have noticed the silence. That last part is the one to get right: too eager and it accuses a bridge that has had no time to dial, too quiet and it deletes the alarm this whole concept exists to raise.

`asked` is the other thing a reading produces, and it is what this watch does rather than what it says. Saying so was all of this at first, and saying so was not enough: a pane whose replacement bridge was decided on and never started has nothing that can ask for another, because everything that asks is driven by a bridge ending and this one never began - so the pane had none for the life of the app process, agent and all (kan a_2KIPfvt7L). The condition was already computed here, exactly, so this names the panes to ask a bridge for as well as the ones to report.

It is the opposite rule to `raised`, and the two are deliberately not the same list, on two counts. A condition that stays true is said once, because a roster that repeated itself is the nagging keying a problem by its condition exists to end; a bridge that never arrived is asked for again, because the last ask is exactly what may have produced nothing. And asking waits three deadlines where saying waits one, because the two cost different amounts of being wrong: a sentence about a pane that turns out fine is withdrawn a moment later, while an ask tears down the surface its bridge is the command of - and one aimed at a bridge that was merely slow replaces it with one just as slow on a machine just as busy. Every overdue pane appears in `asked`, including ones whose bridges are ending on their own - this watch only knows that nothing is dialing, and `respawn` is what decides whether asking is the right answer for a pane that gave up or was yielded to another window.

That is also why `next_wake` is rarely null while a pane is dark. Asking has to keep happening, so the loop keeps waking for as long as a drawn pane has no bridge, rather than sleeping forever the moment its problem is raised.

A pane key is `<daemon>/<the name Muster minted>`, and a remedy carries the name alone, because that is what the CLI's `--pane` takes.

cases.name: a pane whose bridge never dials is reported once the deadline passes
cases.why: The base case, and the whole point: before this the same fact reached the run log and the window said nothing, so the first person to know was whoever typed into a pane that looked fine. The sentence is pinned here rather than in every case because it is one sentence - the deadline in it rather than the elapsed time, so that a condition which stays true has nothing new to say on the next reading. A reattach is offered beside it as a button, because it only asks sooner for the bridge Muster asks for on its own.

expect.detail: The pane local/p1w3r07bsd has had a socket open for over 5s, and no bridge has attached - the bridge that draws this pane either never started or cannot reach the socket or its daemon. The pane shows what it last drew and nothing typed into it appears, so it looks frozen rather than broken; every other pane in the window is unaffected. Muster asks for another bridge every 15s and keeps asking; `muster pane reattach --pane p1w3r07bsd` asks now. The run log has the cause: look for `link.accept.failed`, `bridge.exited.reported` and `pane.channel.unavailable`.

cases.name: a pane taken over by another bridge says which window has it
cases.why: Nothing is broken here and the sentence must not read as though something is: another window asked for this pane and the daemon gave it to them, which is the arrangement the daemon allows. What the person needs is where their pane went and how to get it back, and neither is derivable from a blank pane. No button is offered: a reattach here takes the pane back from the window showing it, which is a decision the sentence describes rather than a click to make by accident.

steps.reason: another bridge attached to this pane

expect.detail: Another bridge attached to the pane local/p1w3r07bsd and took it over, so this window has stopped drawing it - most often a second Muster window that was opened onto the same machine. The daemon lets one bridge draw a pane at a time, so nothing here can show it while that one does; the agent itself is untouched and every other pane in this window is unaffected. Whichever window is showing it now is the one to work in. To bring it back here instead, run `muster pane reattach --pane p1w3r07bsd` - that asks for a bridge, and a bridge after the first takes the pane over the way the other window's did.

cases.name: a pane whose attach was refused says a reattach takes it over
cases.why: The failure that cost a working day under herdr, and the one nobody guesses: a stream whose transport died stays open on the far machine until its ssh notices, so the first attach after a relaunch is refused by a machine that is otherwise perfectly healthy. Every replacement bridge takes the pane over, so this is usually gone by the time anyone reads it - and when it is not, what brings the pane back is asking for another bridge, which is the one remedy the sentence names. It stays a sentence rather than a button, because that bridge takes the pane from whatever is drawing it, which may be a window somebody is looking at (kan a_2IQsToWVW).

steps.reason: another bridge is drawing this pane; attach with takeover to replace it

expect.detail: The pane devenv/p206y9rm8s has been dark for over 5s: something else was drawing it when this window asked, and the daemon lets one bridge draw a pane at a time. The agent behind it is untouched and every other pane in the window is unaffected. `muster pane reattach --pane p206y9rm8s` takes it over from whatever holds it.

cases.name: a pane whose connection went says which machine to check
cases.why: A dropped VPN, and the case that recovers on its own once the machine is reachable - so the sentence has to say that rather than send somebody looking for a fault. It also has to say the agent is untouched, because a pane frozen on its last frame reads as work lost. A reattach is offered beside it: what last drew the pane was this window's own bridge, and against a machine still away it only fails again.

steps.reason: the stream from the daemon broke

expect.detail: The pane devenv/p206y9q4kd lost the connection carrying it and has not got one back within 5s. It shows what it last painted and takes no keystrokes; the agent behind it is untouched, and panes on other machines in this window are unaffected. Check that the machine holding it is reachable - the run log says `tunnel.down` when the connection is the reason, and Muster keeps asking for a bridge until one dials. `muster pane reattach --pane p206y9q4kd` asks now, once the machine is back.

cases.name: a pane that no longer exists is owed nothing
cases.why: What a bridge hears when its pane is closed under it: the daemon says the pane is gone. The window can still be drawing the pane when this arrives, and a wait started here once accused the network five seconds later - 'check that the machine holding it is reachable' - about a pane somebody had just closed on a healthy machine (kan a_2LMpvavhA). Nothing can attach to it, so there is nothing to wait for, nothing to say and nothing to ask for.

cases.name: a pane still inside its deadline is not accused
cases.why: A bridge takes measurable time to start, dial and paint, and a window that reported every pane during its first moments would be a window nobody reads. The deadline separates slow from broken, so the boundary is exclusive on the near side - and one nanosecond short of it, the answer is to wait that nanosecond.

cases.name: the same overdue pane is not news on the second reading
cases.why: The watch runs on a clock, so it asks repeatedly about a condition that stays true. If every reading counted as news the roster would republish and reopen itself for as long as the pane stayed quiet - which is the nagging that keying a problem by its condition was meant to end.

cases.name: a bridge that dials in late takes the problem back
cases.why: A pane reported after five seconds whose bridge turns up at six is a working pane, and the box disappearing is the only confirmation anybody gets that it started working. Leaving it raised would teach whoever saw it to stop believing the roster.

cases.name: a pane closed while overdue takes its problem with it
cases.why: The case that goes wrong when it is forgotten. A pane that was deaf and is now gone would otherwise leave an error in the roster naming something nobody can look at, and no later event would ever clear it - the pane it was about is the thing that no longer exists.

cases.name: one deaf pane among working ones is reported precisely
cases.why: Fourteen panes working and one deaf is the case worth reporting exactly, and it is why the condition is keyed per pane rather than per window. A window-wide answer would either accuse the working panes or say nothing while one of them swallowed everything typed into it.

cases.name: two daemons handing out the same pane id are two panes
cases.why: Both daemons in a window call their first pane w1:p1, so anything keyed by pane alone lets one machine's pane answer for the other's. The key carries the daemon for the same reason every other cross-daemon key in the core does.

cases.name: a bridge that exited starts the wait again
cases.why: A pane keeps its channel while its surface is thrown away and built again, so the replacement bridge has to dial too. The seam's bridge_link.rs names this as the reason its accept loop runs more than once, and a replacement that never arrives is the same dark pane - so the clock restarts rather than the pane being considered settled for good.

cases.name: a reported pane whose bridge ends is taken back and said again once the new wait runs out
cases.why: A bridge ending restarts the wait, because the replacement has to dial too, and the sentence the pane gets next knows how the last bridge ended. So the problem raised before is taken back and raised again a deadline later, and the clear says the wait started over - which is what a run log reader needs in order not to read it as the pane having recovered.

cases.name: a deadline of zero watches nothing
cases.why: The honest answer for a run with no bridges to wait for, and what the seam's own knob means when it is set to 0. Off has to mean off rather than nearly-immediately: a zero read as a deadline that has always passed would accuse every pane the moment its socket was bound.

cases.name: nothing waiting means nothing to wake up for
cases.why: An idle window should cost no wakeups at all, which is what lets the watch be a parked thread rather than a tick. This is the answer that decides it.

cases.name: the wake is the earliest deadline among the panes waiting
cases.why: So that a caller holding a real clock sleeps exactly as long as it has to, rather than polling. The earliest, because a pane opened later must not push back the report of one opened earlier.

cases.name: a pane already reported does not decide when to wake next
cases.why: The first of two ways a loop around this misbehaves. Nothing further happens to a reported pane on the clock alone - only a bridge dialing in or the pane closing changes its answer, and both of those tell the caller directly - so counting it would answer zero forever and spin. What decides here is the pane still waiting behind it. The asking does not decide it either, here: this pane was asked for at the reading above, so it wants waking a whole deadline later and the pane still inside its own is sooner.

cases.name: an overdue pane nobody has reported yet wants waking immediately
cases.why: The other way it goes wrong. A pane that fell overdue while the caller was busy publishing something else must not be slept through, because on a quiet window nothing else would ever wake it - so the answer is zero rather than nothing, until it has actually been reported.

cases.name: a pane nobody is drawing is not accused of swallowing anything
cases.why: What this raises is that a pane renders and discards everything typed into it. A pane no region is showing renders nothing, so the sentence is false about it however long its socket has been bound. The zoomed tab is where it was noticed - a window opening onto one bound a socket per pane and then accused the three the zoom covered, on every launch, as a notification each - but the rule is not about zoom: it is that an accusation nobody could have observed is not an observation.

cases.name: a pane that stops being drawn takes its problem back
cases.why: Switching tabs, or zooming one, must not leave an error standing about a pane nobody can look at - that is the same stale accusation as an error outliving a closed pane, and it reaches a person as a notification. The pane keeps its channel through this, because its surface is parked rather than released and its bridge may still be dialed into that socket; what it loses is the claim being made about it.

cases.name: a pane drawn again waits a whole deadline from the moment it is drawn
cases.why: The half of this that goes wrong quietly, and the one worth pinning hardest. A pane's clock runs while nobody is looking at it, so carrying that reading forward would accuse a bridge the instant its pane is drawn, for a silence nobody was in a position to notice. Here the pane is hidden with almost its whole deadline spent and comes back: a reading one nanosecond short of a full deadline from its return says nothing, and the wake it asks for is the remainder rather than zero.

cases.name: a pane drawn again and still deaf does say so
cases.why: The other side of the restart, and the reason it is a restart rather than an exemption. A pane hidden while its bridge died and then brought back on screen is a pane somebody is now typing into - so the alarm has to arrive, one full deadline after it was drawn and not before. Getting this wrong in the quiet direction would delete the alarm rather than correct it, which is worse than the false ones this began as.

cases.name: nothing on screen is nothing to wake up for
cases.why: A window showing none of the panes it is holding open - every tab off screen, or a launch that has not drawn anything yet - owes nothing on the clock, so an idle window costs no wakeups. Without this the loop would ask again at every deadline about panes nobody can see.

cases.name: a pane nothing has dialed is asked for again each time its bridge was started
cases.why:
The recovery, and the shape that makes it one. The first ask is exactly the one that may have produced a bridge that never dials, so a watch that asked once would be a watch that noticed the bug and did nothing about it. Each started bridge that has not dialed three deadlines later is asked for again, while the sentence is said once - the two halves of a reading answer opposite rules on purpose.

The two clocks behind that are also why the problem is not cleared and raised again here. How long the pane has been deaf is what the sentence is about and keeps climbing; how long ago the shell started the last bridge is what paces the asking, and restarts on every start. Sharing one number would make a pane stop being overdue the moment it was asked for, and the roster would clear and re-raise its problem every deadline for as long as the pane stayed dark.

The last ask is not started, so there is nothing more on the clock: `next_wake` is null.

cases.name: a reading before the asking is due asks for nothing
cases.why: What paces the asking, and why it is not counted from the moment the sentence is. A window republishes for its own reasons - a pane opening, a problem being raised - and every one of those wakes this loop, so a reading that asked whenever a pane was overdue would tear down and rebuild a surface as fast as anything else in the window moved.

cases.name: a pane drawn again is not asked for until it has waited
cases.why: The same rule the sentence follows, and a longer wait. A pane's clock ran while nobody could see it, so a window switching tabs would otherwise tear down and rebuild the surface of every pane it brought on screen - on the strength of a silence nobody was in a position to notice. This pane is reported, because it has been drawn and deaf for longer than a deadline; it is not asked for, because asking waits three of them and its bridge may simply be slow.

cases.name: a bridge that is merely slow is left to arrive
cases.why: The way this recovery could make things worse, written down where it can fail. An ask tears down the surface its bridge is the command of, so one aimed at a bridge that was about to dial kills a working bridge and replaces it with one just as slow on a machine just as busy. A loaded machine is exactly the condition this whole feature was written for - the incident behind it had a load average of 185 - so the pane is reported at one deadline and left alone until three have passed.

cases.name: an ask the shell has not started is not asked for again
cases.why: What a loaded machine did to the asking: the watch counted nine asks in two minutes that a shell running minutes behind never reached, and replaced bridges that were only slow to spawn (kan a_2YBZU4Ujx). The shell builds a bridge only when the number a view carries for the pane moves, so an ask it has not reached is still waiting for it, and a second one changes nothing it will see sooner - it only replaces the bridge it is about to start. So a pane whose socket is bound and whose shell has not said it started a bridge is reported like any other, and is not asked for, however long it waits.

cases.name: the asking is timed from when the shell started the bridge
cases.why: The other half of the same card. A bridge started twelve seconds after it was asked for has had three seconds to dial at the moment an ask timed from the ask would replace it. Timed from the start, it gets the same three deadlines as any other bridge; the sentence is still timed from when the pane went deaf, because that is what it is about.

cases.name: a person asks even while the last ask has not been started
cases.why: The way back for a shell that got an ask and never started a bridge. Nothing automatic asks about that pane again, by the rule above, so `muster pane reattach` has to: a person is always asked for. So is a replacement for a bridge that ended, because a bridge ending means the shell started one whether or not its report has arrived. Only Muster asking on its own is held back.

cases.name: a surface torn down after its new bridge started keeps the start
cases.why: The notice that a surface went and the report that its replacement started arrive in no fixed order. Read as a fresh ask, a late notice would leave the pane waiting on a start that has already happened, and nothing automatic would ask about it again. So the wait restarts and the start stands.

cases.name: a daemon that answers again asks for its panes nothing dialed, and not for the others
cases.why: The moment a bridge can attach again (kan a_2YQD5xCFq). A pane on that daemon whose last bridge was started has failed or will, so it is named for an ask. One whose ask the shell has not started yet is not: that bridge will start against a daemon that answers. A pane on another machine keeps its own wait, which is why the next wake is its deadline, 3.5s on, rather than a whole deadline from the reconnect.

cases.name: a connection that is back is not blamed for a pane still dark
cases.why: A wait that carried a lost connection said to check that the machine was reachable, and said it four seconds after it was (kan a_2YQD5xCFq). Once the daemon answers again that sentence is false, so one already said is taken back, and a pane still dark a deadline later says only that nothing has dialed.

expect.detail: The pane devenv/p206y9p61r has had a socket open for over 5s, and no bridge has attached - the bridge that draws this pane either never started or cannot reach the socket or its daemon. The pane shows what it last drew and nothing typed into it appears, so it looks frozen rather than broken; every other pane in the window is unaffected. Muster asks for another bridge every 15s and keeps asking; `muster pane reattach --pane p206y9p61r` asks now.
